chapters.title: Chapter 3: Debt Markets and Interest Rates

lessons.title: The RBI Repo Rate and Why Your Company's Borrowing Cost Changes

children.text: Every two months, six people sit in Mumbai and decide a single number. Within weeks that number changes your company's interest bill, your home loan EMI and what your fixed deposit earns. This lesson traces the full path from that decision to your desk.
What the Repo Rate Actually Is

markDefs.definition: The rate at which RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks against government securities. It is the anchor rate for the entire Indian interest rate system.
The Monetary Policy Committee: the six-member body that decides India's policy rate, with three RBI members and three external members.
The process by which a change in the policy rate flows through to deposit rates, lending rates and bond yields across the economy. It is neither instant nor complete.

children.text: The
repo rate
is what banks pay to borrow short-term money from RBI. It is decided by the
Monetary Policy Committee

, whose legal mandate is to keep inflation near a target while supporting growth. Because it sets the price at which the safest lender in the system provides money, every other rate in the economy is built on top of it, through a process called
monetary transmission

stats.label: Inflation Target
stats.context: Consumer price inflation, under the statutory framework

stats.label: Tolerance Band
stats.context: Sustained breaches require RBI to explain itself to the government

stats.label: MPC Members
stats.context: Three from RBI, three external; the Governor has a casting vote in a tie

body.text: RBI is not targeting your EMI, your company's interest bill or the stock market. It is targeting inflation. Everything else, including what you pay on your loan, is a side effect of that single objective.

body.caption: The Toolkit, Beyond the Headline Rate

cells: The rate at which RBI lends to banks
Borrowing gets costlier across the system
The rate banks earn for parking surplus funds with RBI
Sets the floor under short-term market rates
Share of deposits banks must keep with RBI in cash
Less money available to lend, tightening liquidity directly
Share of deposits banks must hold in government securities
Constrains how much banks can deploy elsewhere
RBI buying or selling government bonds
Selling drains cash from the system and pushes yields up
Guidance on the likely direction of future rates
Moves market expectations and bond yields before any rate changes

body.text: Markets often move more on the stance and the tone of the statement than on the rate decision itself. A policy that holds the repo rate unchanged but signals future tightening can push bond yields up the same afternoon, because lenders price the future, not the present.

children.text: The Transmission Chain, Step by Step

body.title: From a Mumbai Decision to Your Company's Interest Bill

events.title: The MPC Raises the Repo Rate
events.description: Say the committee hikes by 0.50 percentage points to cool persistent inflation, and signals that more may follow.

events.title: Bond Yields Move First
events.description: Government bond yields adjust within minutes, because bonds trade continuously and traders reprice instantly. Corporate bond yields follow, since they are priced as a spread over government bonds.

events.title: Externally Benchmarked Loans Reprice
events.description: Floating rate loans linked directly to the repo rate move at their next reset, which is typically quarterly. Retail and small business borrowers feel this fastest.

events.title: Bank Cost of Funds Rises
events.description: Banks must offer more on deposits to retain them, which lifts their internal cost of funds and therefore their internally benchmarked lending rates.

events.title: Corporate Loans Reprice
events.description: Term loans and working capital limits reset at their contractual dates. Commercial paper reprices at each fresh issuance, so it moves sooner.

events.title: Real Decisions Change
events.description: Projects with thin returns get deferred, inventory is trimmed, hiring slows and consumers postpone big purchases funded by loans.

events.title: Inflation Responds
events.description: Slower demand eventually cools price rises. The long lag is exactly why RBI acts on its forecast rather than on today's inflation print.

body.title: Why Your Loan Rate Lags the Policy Rate (Illustrative)

body.text: Notice which line moves last. Loan rates typically reprice faster than deposit rates when rates rise, and deposit rates often fall faster than loan rates when rates are cut. Borrowers feel a hike quickly; savers wait for the benefit. This is not a conspiracy, it is the contractual structure of the two products, but it is worth knowing when you plan either side.

body.title: Externally Benchmarked vs Internally Benchmarked Loans

columns.label: Externally Benchmarked (Repo-Linked)
points: The rate is tied directly to an external benchmark such as the repo rate
Resets at contractual intervals, typically once a quarter
Moves transparently and quickly in both directions
Standard for most new floating rate retail and small business loans
You can verify the change yourself: benchmark plus a fixed spread

columns.label: Internally Benchmarked (Such as MCLR)
points: The rate is tied to the bank's own computed cost of funds
Resets at longer agreed intervals, often six months or a year
Moves with a lag, and not always in step with policy
Common in older loans and many corporate facilities
Harder to audit from outside, since the inputs are the bank's own

body.title: Who Feels It First?
body.question: RBI hikes the repo rate by 0.50 percentage points. Which of these is most likely to reprice first?
options: A five-year fixed rate corporate bond issued last year
A home loan linked to an external benchmark, at its next quarterly reset
A term loan priced off the bank's internal benchmark with an annual reset
A three-year fixed deposit opened six months ago
body.explanation: Externally benchmarked floating rate loans reset quickly, typically each quarter. Internally benchmarked loans wait for their longer reset date. Instruments with a fixed rate, whether a bond or a deposit, do not reprice at all until they mature, which is precisely what fixing a rate buys you.

children.text: What Half a Percentage Point Actually Costs
Take a ₹50 lakh home loan running for 20 years, on a floating rate that moves from 8.5% to 9%. Half a percentage point sounds trivial until you run it.

stats.label: EMI at 9.0%
stats.context: The same loan, after a 0.50 point rise

stats.label: Extra Over 20 Years
stats.context: If the higher rate persists for the full tenure

body.text: Most Indian banks respond to a rate hike by extending your loan tenure rather than raising the EMI, because a longer tenure is less painful to communicate. Your monthly outflow looks unchanged while you quietly pay for several more years. Ask your bank which of the two they changed, because you usually have the right to choose.

body.title: Now Size It for Your Employer
body.prompt: Your company carries ₹40 crore of floating rate debt. After a policy cycle, its lending rate rises by 0.75 percentage points. What is the extra annual interest cost, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: ₹40 crore × 0.75% = ₹0.30 crore = ₹30 lakh a year. For a company earning ₹10 crore of annual profit, that is 3% of profit gone, with no change in sales, costs or headcount. This is why CFOs care about the policy statement more than most employees realise.

body.title: Why Would RBI Deliberately Make Borrowing Expensive?

children.text: Raising rates slows the economy on purpose. That is the point, and there are four reasons a central bank accepts that cost:
Inflation is a tax on everyone.
It hits salaried and low-income households hardest, because their incomes adjust slowly while food and fuel prices do not wait.
Expectations are self-fulfilling.
If businesses expect prices to keep rising, they raise prices pre-emptively and workers demand higher wages, which makes inflation persistent. Acting early is cheaper than acting late.
The rupee is in play.
If Indian rates fall too far below rates abroad, foreign capital can leave in search of better returns, weakening the rupee and making imports costlier, which itself feeds inflation.
Cheap money creates its own risks.
Sustained low rates encourage over-borrowing and asset price bubbles, which are far more expensive to clean up than to prevent.
The trade-off is genuine and uncomfortable. Every rate hike that protects the value of a salary also makes a loan costlier for the same person.

body.title: The Morning After a Rate Hike
body.scenario: You are an L&D manager at a mid-sized consumer durables company in Ahmedabad. RBI hikes the repo rate by 0.50 percentage points. Within a week, the CFO defers a planned plant upgrade, sales flags that dealer financing has become costlier, and two team members ask whether their home loan EMIs will change.
body.prompt: Explain what connects all three of these, and what you can and cannot tell your colleagues.
body.modelAnswer: All three trace back to the same decision. The CFO deferred capex because the project was evaluated against the cost of borrowing; when that cost rises, projects with returns close to the borrowing rate stop making sense, so they are postponed rather than funded at a loss. Dealer financing became costlier because dealers and their customers borrow on floating rate facilities that reprice with the benchmark, which reduces how much stock dealers are willing to hold and how readily customers buy on EMI, so the company's sales pipeline tightens even though its product and pricing have not changed. The home loan question is the same mechanism at a personal level: loans linked to an external benchmark reset at contractual intervals, usually quarterly, so the EMI or the tenure will change at the next reset. What you can tell colleagues is factual and general: check whether their loan is externally or internally benchmarked, find the reset date and the spread in their sanction letter, and ask the bank whether the EMI or the tenure is being adjusted, since they usually have a right to choose. What you should not do is advise anyone to prepay, refinance or switch lenders, because that depends on personal cash flows and is advice you are not qualified to give. Pointing people to their own loan documents and their bank is the responsible line.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The rate at which RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks, and the anchor for interest rates across the economy, is the ___ rate.
body.explanation: The repo rate is the policy anchor. Every other rate, from your savings account to a AAA corporate bond, is priced at some distance above or below it, depending on risk and tenor.

body.title: Check Your Own Loan After Any Policy Change
steps: Find whether your loan is linked to an external benchmark or to the bank's internal rate, which is stated in the sanction letter
Note the spread over the benchmark, since that is the part the bank sets and the part you can sometimes negotiate
Find the reset date, because that is when a policy change actually reaches you
After a hike, ask the bank whether they changed your EMI or extended your tenure, and confirm which one you prefer
Compare your effective rate with what the same bank offers new borrowers, since long-standing customers often sit on wider spreads

body.label: RBI: Monetary Policy Statements
body.description: The MPC resolution and the Governor's statement are published on the day of the decision. Reading the resolution once takes ten minutes and tells you more than a week of market commentary about it.

points: The repo rate is what banks pay to borrow from RBI, and it anchors every other interest rate in the economy
The six-member MPC sets it with a legal mandate to keep inflation near target, not to manage EMIs, profits or the stock market
Transmission runs from bond yields within minutes, to benchmarked loans within a quarter, to real business decisions over several quarters
Externally benchmarked loans reprice quickly and transparently, while internally benchmarked loans lag
Loan rates usually rise faster than deposit rates, so borrowers feel tightening before savers feel the benefit
Half a percentage point on a ₹50 lakh home loan is about ₹1,595 a month, and 0.75 points on ₹40 crore of corporate debt is ₹30 lakh a year
After a hike, check whether your bank raised your EMI or extended your tenure, because the second option is easy to miss

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial, borrowing or investment advice. All rates, EMI figures and timelines used are illustrative teaching examples, not current market levels or predictions. Monetary policy tools, benchmarks and reset norms are set by RBI and change over time, so verify current rules with your lender or on RBI's website.
